τόπον. πλὴν οὐκ ἄτοπόν ἐστι τῷ ῥητῷ χρήσασθαί ποτε πρὸς τοὺς οἰομένους μετὰ τὴν
πίστιν δεῖν περιτέμνεσθαι ἐξ εὐλαβείας, εὐλαβείας δὲ τῆς οὐ κατ' ἐπίγνω ιν, διὰ τὰ
ἀναγεγραμμένα ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ διαθήκῃ περὶ περιτομῆς. πάλιν οὐ καλόν ἐστι διά τινας
τοὺς ἐκ περιτομῆς πιστεύοντας <καὶ> οἰομένους αἰσχύνην φέρειν αὐτοῖς τὴν
περιτομήν, καὶ βουλομένους ἀκροβυστίαν περισπᾶσθαι, χρῆσθαι ῥητῷ τῷ λέγοντι
Περιτετμημένος τις ἐκλήθη; μὴ ἐπισπάσθω; καὶ ἔχει γε λόγον λέγειν πρὸς τοὺς
τοιούτους, ὅτι κατ' αὐτὸ ἡ περιτομὴ πρᾶγμα ἀδιάφορόν ἐστιν. οὔτε οὖν περὶ
περιτομῆς νῦν ἐστιν οὔτε περὶ ἀκροβυστίας, ἀλλὰ περὶ τοῦ ἀγάμου καὶ τοῦ
γεγαμηκότος· Περιτετμημένος τις ἐκλήθη; μὴ ἐπισπάσθω· ὡσεὶ ἔλεγεν Μὴ
ἐπισπάσθω γυναῖκα· ἤδη περιετμήθη· ἀπέβαλεν γυναῖκα, μὴ γαμείτω ἄλλην. Ἐν
ἀκροβυστίᾳ ἐκλήθη τις; μὴ περιτεμνέσθω· οἷον· Ἐν γάμῳ ἐκλήθης; μὴ ἀπόβαλέ σου
τὴν γυναῖκα. Ἡ περιτομὴ οὐδέν ἐστι, καὶ ἡ ἀκροβυστία οὐδέν ἐστιν. ἐπεὶ τινὲς
οἴονται τὸν ἄγαμον πλέον τι ἔχειν κατὰ τοῦτο τοῦ γεγαμηκότος, τὸν δὲ γεγαμηκότα
ἧττόν τι ἔχειν παρ' αὐτὸ τὸ γεγαμηκέναι τοῦ ἀγάμου, θέλομεν, φησί, διδάξαι ὅτι τῷ
ἰδίῳ λόγῳ ἡ ἀγαμία ἀδιάφορόν ἐστιν καὶ τῷ ἰδίῳ λόγῳ ὁ γάμος ἀδιάφορό<ν> ἐστιν.
δύναται γὰρ καὶ ὁ ἄγαμος ὢν καὶ ἀληθῶς καθαρεύων ἀπὸ πάσης μίξεως, ἄλλως δὲ
κακῶς βιούς, μὴ ὠφελεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγαμίας· δύναται δέ τις καὶ ἐν γάμῳ ὢν καὶ τὰ
τοῦ γάμου πράττων τάξει δὲ καὶ καιρῷ αὐτὰ ποιῶν, τὴν ἄλλην πολιτείαν σώζων, μὴ
ἐλάττων εἶναι τοῦ ἀγάμου. ὅτι γὰρ ἀδιάφορόν ἐστιν ἡ ἀγαμία καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ καθαρότης,
οὕτως ἀποδείξομεν. εἰ μὲν μόνοι οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἤσκουν τὴν ἀγαμίαν, ἦν ἂν
εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἡ ἀγαμία τῷ ἰδίῳ λόγῳ καθαρόν τι καὶ θεῖον πρᾶγμά ἐστιν· νῦν δὲ ἔστιν
εὑρεῖν καὶ μοχθηρᾷ προθέσει ἀγάμους. οἱ γοῦν ἀπὸ Μαρκίωνος ἀσκοῦσι καὶ αὐτοὶ

pass_a_gloss: Here as well he labels “slave” the person called after marrying, and “free” the unmarried. Talk of circumcision and of slaves therefore aims at this topic. Still one may at times aim the verse at people who after believing think they must be circumcised from a reverence that is not according to knowledge, because the old covenant writes about circumcision. Again it is unwise, because some circumcised believers feel shame at circumcision and want to draw a foreskin, to lean on “Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised.” One can tell them circumcision by itself is morally neutral. So the present subject is neither cutting nor foreskin but married versus unmarried: “Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised” means roughly “do not take a wife again; he already put a wife away; he must not marry another.” “Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised” means “you were called while married; do not dismiss your wife.” Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Because some think the unmarried holds an edge over the married, and the married a deficit merely by marrying, he wants to show that celibacy by itself is neutral and marriage by itself is neutral. An unmarried person truly free of every mixture may still live badly otherwise and gain nothing from celibacy; a married person handling marriage in due order and season while keeping the rest of life may stand no lower than the unmarried. That celibacy and purity are themselves neutral we show thus. If only church people practiced celibacy, one might call celibacy by itself pure and divine; but one also finds celibates with a base aim. Marcionites practice celibacy and purity too, yet not as church people: church people please the Creator, Marcionites refuse to aid the world’s god. Church life, word, clean knowledge, and truth adorn celibacy. So the unmarried state is neutral by itself; and a married person can also live without blame, as already shown. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, both by the letter and by the theme. What saves? Keeping God’s commands. Whoever looses one least command and teaches others so is not said to be shut out of the heavens’ kingdom but called least in it. If loosing one least command makes someone least in that kingdom, where does the person who loosed two stand? So each must stay in the calling where he was called. Called while married? Do not envy the unmarried. Called unmarried? Do not rush to marry if you can live more purely. Called as a slave? Do not fret; yet if you can become free, use that instead. The slave called in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman; likewise the free person called is Christ’s slave. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of people. Brothers, each must stay with God in the condition of his calling. pass_b_english: this also here he names a slave the one called after marriage, and free the unmarried. What is said about circumcision and about slaves is therefore said with a view to the place. Yet it is not out of place sometimes to use the saying against those who think after the faith one must be circumcised from a reverence—yet a reverence not according to knowledge—because of what is written in the old covenant about circumcision. Again it is not good, because of certain ones from circumcision who believe and think circumcision brings them shame and wish to draw a foreskin, to use the saying that says: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. And there is reason to say to such that in itself circumcision is a matter of indifference. So now it is neither about circumcision nor about uncircumcision, but about the unmarried and the married: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised—as if he were saying: Let him not draw a wife; he has already been circumcised; he put away a wife; let him not marry another. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised—as if: You were called in marriage; do not put away your wife. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. Since some think the unmarried has something more in this respect than the married, and the married something less than the unmarried by the very fact of having married, we wish, he says, to teach that in its own account celibacy is indifferent and in its own account marriage is indifferent. For the one who is unmarried and truly pure from every mixture, yet living badly in other ways, may gain no benefit from celibacy; and someone in marriage, doing the things of marriage in order and season, keeping the rest of the way of life, may be no less than the unmarried. That celibacy itself and purity itself are indifferent we will prove thus. If only those from the church practiced celibacy, one might say that celibacy in its own account is something pure and divine; but now one can find also those unmarried with a base intention. Those from Marcion also practice celibacy and purity, but not as the church’s people do; for these do so to please the God who created the world, those so as not to cooperate with the god of the world. Celibacy is adorned by an ecclesiastical life and word, by pure knowledge and truth. So also the unmarried is indifferent in his own account; and it is possible also for one in marriage to be without blame, as we have already given. Circumcision then is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, both according to the wording and according to what is set before us. But what is it that saves? Keeping God’s commandments. For everyone who looses one of these least commandments and teaches people so—he did not say will not enter the kingdom of the heavens but will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens (Matthew 5:19). And if the one who loosed one of the least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens, where will the one who loosed two commandments be found? Let each therefore remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called in marriage? Do not envy the unmarried. Were you called unmarried? Do not by all means draw a foreskin, if you are able to live more purely.

Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned about it; but if you are also able to become free, rather use it. For the one called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise the one called free is Christ’s slave. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Brothers, let each remain with God in that in which he was called (1 Corinthians 7:21–24). He named a slave of necessity the married man; for the husband is a slave of the wife, not having authority over his own body, and the wife of the husband; for she does not have authority over her own body, but the husband.
